title: The Man of God and the Altar
overview: 1 Kings 13 recounts a dramatic narrative involving a man of God from Judah who confronts King Jeroboam at the altar in Bethel. The chapter highlights divine judgment, prophetic authority, and the consequences of disobedience. The man of God delivers a prophecy against the idolatrous altar, accompanied by a miraculous sign, yet later falls into deception and disobedience, resulting in his death. This chapter underscores the seriousness of obeying God's commands and the dangers of false prophecy. It also reveals the persistence of Jeroboam's sinful practices despite clear warnings, setting a tone of judgment that affects his dynasty. The chapter serves as a sobering reminder of God's holiness and the necessity of faithfulness in ministry and leadership.
structure:
**Verses 1-6: The Prophecy and Sign Against the Altar.** A man of God from Judah prophesies against the altar at Bethel, predicting Josiah's future judgment and demonstrating God's power through a miraculous sign that the altar will be torn apart and ashes poured out. King Jeroboam's hand withers when he attempts to seize the prophet but is restored after prayer.

**Verses 7-10: The Man of God's Refusal to Eat or Drink.** Jeroboam invites the man of God to his house, but the prophet refuses, citing God's command not to eat, drink, or return by the same route.

**Verses 11-19: The Deception of the Old Prophet.** An old prophet from Bethel hears of the man of God's actions, pursues him, and lies by claiming an angel instructed him to bring the man of God back to eat and drink, leading to the prophet's disobedience.

**Verses 20-26: The Judgment on the Man of God.** God pronounces judgment on the man of God for disobedience, predicting he will not be buried in his ancestral tomb. He is killed by a lion, fulfilling the prophecy.

**Verses 27-32: The Burial and Prophecy of the Old Prophet.** The old prophet retrieves the body, buries it, and prophesies the certainty of the judgment against the altar and high places.

**Verses 33-34: The Continued Sin of Jeroboam.** Despite the warnings, Jeroboam persists in his idolatry, consecrating unqualified priests, which becomes a sin leading to the destruction of his house.

keyVerses.text: And he cried against the altar in the word of the LORD, and said, O altar, altar, thus saith the LORD; Behold, a child shall be born unto the house of David, Josiah by name; and upon thee shall he offer the priests of the high places that burn incense upon thee, and men's bones shall be burnt upon thee.
keyVerses.significance: This verse contains the prophetic judgment against the idolatrous altar, foretelling King Josiah's future reforms and God's judgment on false worship. It highlights God's sovereignty over history and His commitment to purify worship.

keyVerses.text: For so was it charged me by the word of the LORD, saying, Eat no bread, nor drink water, nor turn again by the same way that thou camest.
keyVerses.significance: This verse reveals the strict divine command given to the man of God, emphasizing obedience to God's instructions as essential for prophetic ministry. It sets the stage for the tragic disobedience that follows.

keyVerses.text: But camest back, and hast eaten bread and drunk water in the place, of the which the LORD did say to thee, Eat no bread, and drink no water; thy carcase shall not come unto the sepulchre of thy fathers.
keyVerses.significance: This verse pronounces the consequence of the prophet's disobedience, illustrating the seriousness of defying God's commands. It serves as a solemn warning about the cost of failing to obey God fully.

keyVerses.text: And this thing became sin unto the house of Jeroboam, even to cut it off, and to destroy it from off the face of the earth.
keyVerses.significance: This verse summarizes the lasting impact of Jeroboam's idolatry, marking it as a sin that leads to the downfall of his dynasty. It underscores the theme of judgment against persistent rebellion.

characters.name: Man of God from Judah
characters.description: A prophet sent by God to Bethel to deliver a message of judgment against Jeroboam's altar. He performs a miraculous sign but ultimately disobeys God's command due to deception, resulting in his death.

characters.name: King Jeroboam
characters.description: The first king of the northern kingdom of Israel who established idolatrous worship at Bethel. He resists God's warnings and continues in sin, leading to judgment on his house.

characters.name: Old Prophet of Bethel
characters.description: A local prophet who deceives the man of God by falsely claiming an angel instructed him to bring the man of God back to eat and drink, causing the man's disobedience and death.

characters.name: God
characters.description: The sovereign Lord who sends the man of God with a prophetic message, performs miracles, pronounces judgment for disobedience, and upholds His holiness and justice throughout the narrative.

themes.description: The chapter highlights the critical importance of obeying God's explicit commands, as seen in the man of God's initial faithfulness and subsequent fatal disobedience. This theme resonates throughout Scripture as foundational to faithful living.

God's judgment is clearly demonstrated through the withering of Jeroboam's hand, the tearing of the altar, and the death of the man of God. The chapter warns that rebellion against God’s word has serious consequences.
The old prophet's lie about an angel's message introduces the danger of false prophecy and deception, emphasizing the need for discernment and faithfulness to God's revealed word.
Jeroboam's establishment of idolatrous worship and his persistence in sin despite warnings illustrate the destructive power of idolatry and its impact on Israel's spiritual and political future.

historicalContext: This chapter is set during the divided monarchy period of Israel's history, specifically early in the northern kingdom under King Jeroboam I (circa 930 BC). Bethel was one of the main centers of Jeroboam's idolatrous worship, established to prevent his subjects from going to Jerusalem in Judah. The political tension between the northern kingdom of Israel and the southern kingdom of Judah provides the backdrop for this prophetic confrontation. Prophets played a crucial role in Israelite society as God's messengers, often challenging kings and calling for covenant faithfulness. The cultural context included widespread syncretism and unauthorized worship practices, which the Deuteronomic history condemns.

theologicalInterpretations.description: Reformed theologians emphasize the sovereignty of God in this chapter, highlighting that God's commands must be obeyed without compromise. The man of God's disobedience serves as a warning about the seriousness of sin and the necessity of faithfulness to God's revealed word.

Dispensational interpreters often see the man of God's prophecy about Josiah as a clear messianic foreshadowing and emphasize the literal fulfillment of God's judgments. They stress the distinction between God's dealings with Israel and the church, focusing on the prophetic warnings to the nation.

Early church fathers like Augustine interpreted the man of God's disobedience allegorically, seeing it as a lesson on the dangers of yielding to false teaching and the importance of perseverance in faith. They also viewed the altar as symbolic of false worship opposed to true Christian worship.

application: Commit to obeying God's commands fully, recognizing that partial obedience is disobedience.
Be discerning of teachings and claims of divine revelation, testing them against Scripture.
Understand that God's judgment is real and that sin has serious consequences.
Trust in God's sovereignty even when His plans involve discipline or hardship.
Avoid compromising with cultural or religious practices that contradict God's word.
Encourage faithfulness in ministry by relying on God's guidance and not human persuasion.
conclusion: 1 Kings 13 stands as a powerful testimony to the holiness of God and the necessity of complete obedience to His word. Through the story of the man of God and the altar at Bethel, believers are reminded that God's commands are not to be taken lightly, and that deception and disobedience carry grave consequences. The chapter also serves as a warning against idolatry and false teaching, urging Christians to remain steadfast in truth and faithful in their walk with God. Ultimately, it calls for reverence, discernment, and unwavering commitment to God's revealed will.
timeline: c. 930 BC - Early reign of King Jeroboam I in the northern kingdom of Israel

outline.heading: The Prophecy Against the Altar
outline.description: A man of God from Judah proclaims God's judgment against Jeroboam's altar, accompanied by a miraculous sign and the withering of Jeroboam's hand, demonstrating God's power and authority.

outline.heading: The Man of God's Obedience and Departure
outline.description: The man of God refuses Jeroboam's invitation to eat or drink, obeying God's command not to return by the same route, showing initial faithfulness.

outline.heading: The Deception by the Old Prophet
outline.description: An old prophet deceives the man of God with a false claim of an angelic message, leading to the man's disobedience and tragic consequences.

outline.heading: Judgment and Death of the Man of God
outline.description: God pronounces judgment on the man of God for disobedience, resulting in his death by a lion, fulfilling the divine warning.

outline.heading: The Burial and Prophecy of the Old Prophet
outline.description: The old prophet retrieves and buries the body, prophesying the certainty of God's judgment against the altar and idolatrous high places.

outline.heading: Jeroboam's Continued Sin
outline.description: Despite the warnings, Jeroboam persists in idolatry, consecrating unqualified priests, which brings sin and judgment upon his house.
